message.content:
In the classical Greek world the creation and promulgation of laws was carried out by **law‑givers** (Greek: *nomothesoi* – “law‑makers”) and then formally adopted by the political bodies of the polis.  

| Who | What they did | Example |
|-----|---------------|---------|
| **Nomothesoi (law‑givers)** | Drafted and codified the legal code. Their names became synonymous with the laws they produced. | **Draco** (5th c. BCE) – first to write a written code in Athens; **Solon** (early 5th c. BCE) – reformed the Athenian constitution; **Lycurgus** (5th c. BCE) – restructured Spartan society. |
| **Ekklesia (Assembly)** | The citizen assembly that voted on the proposed laws. | Athenian citizens met on the Pnyx to approve or reject the lawgivers’ proposals. |
| **Boule (Council of 500)** | Reviewed, amended, and forwarded the laws to the assembly. | The council drafted legislation and presented it to the Ekklesia. |
| **Archons (chief magistrates)** | Enforced the laws and sometimes had a role in their promulgation. | The Archon Basileus in Athens was the chief executive who signed the laws into effect. |

So, while the **nomothesoi** (law‑givers) were the ones who actually *established* the laws, the formal adoption and enforcement involved the **assembly (ekklesia)**, the **council (boule)**, and the **archons** of each city‑state.
